stories.title: Caring for a dying infant at home
stories.summary: As assistant physician-in-chief in Hayward, he arranged for an immigrant family's dying infant to go home on a respirator, though it was not a covered benefit. For two months he visited twice daily to draw blood and adjust the respirator until the baby died.
stories.quote: She said at the time, that's not a benefit. And I said, yes, but that's what this family needs. So I went to respiratory therapy. I got the equipment.
stories.why: Physician-led care beyond the benefit rules; the act he is proudest of.

stories.title: The troublemaker who won evening appointments
stories.summary: As a young Hayward pediatrician he pushed for appointments at evening and weekend clinics, where families had waited over an hour. Colleagues called him naive, but the system changed and patient experience improved.
stories.quote: We have to give people appointments at night and on the weekends. And some of the rest of the department said, oh, no, you're just naive, you're stupid. That's ridiculous.
stories.why: Shows how making noise about service led to his first leadership role.

stories.title: The Federation's Security Council model
stories.summary: To found the Permanente Federation, the large medical groups had to be reassured they would not be outvoted. The executive committee gave the two California groups seats alongside two at-large members from the smaller groups.
stories.quote: It was what I'd like to sort of call the United Nations Security Council model. The large medical groups were worried that they would be outvoted by the small medical groups
stories.why: A vivid explanation of how the Federation balanced power among medical groups.

stories.title: Why isn't Colorado's success everywhere?
stories.summary: At Health Plan board meetings, medical groups regularly presented quality innovations, and the board asked why they were not spread across the program. That question helped lead to the Care Management Institute.
stories.quote: If you're doing this so well in Colorado, and we applaud you, why is it not the same throughout the organization? Don't we owe all of our members the same standards of quality of care?
stories.why: Origin story for spreading best practices across regions.

stories.title: Coming back every month until told not to
stories.summary: When Orange County's new centralized appointment call center collapsed at launch, Ken Bell asked Ellison to help fix it. He and administrator Priscilla Daniel visited every office monthly to listen until things improved over about a year and a half, and the model spread across KP.
stories.quote: I will come back next month, and the month after that, and the month after that, and the month after that, until you tell me, I don't need to come here anymore.
stories.why: A concrete lesson in change management and listening to the front lines.

stories.title: The receptionist who saves lives
stories.summary: A receptionist persuaded Mary Gonzalez, in for allergies, to book an overdue mammogram, which found an early cancer. Ellison uses it to show that every point of contact in an integrated system can close care gaps.
stories.quote: She could say, my job is not just to check in patients, my job is to save lives.
stories.why: Shows integrated care and prevention through one patient's experience.

stories.title: Ken Bell tells him to stay
stories.summary: Early in his career, as his father was dying back east, Ellison planned to return to work. His area medical director, Ken Bell, told him to stay, and he was with his father when he died while colleagues covered his patients.
stories.quote: And he said, "no, you're not. You're staying right where you are. You're where you need to be, where you're supposed to be.
stories.why: Illustrates collegial support he called the family of the medical group.

stories.title: Turning surgical drapes into COVID masks
stories.summary: Short of protective equipment early in COVID, SCPMG had a surplus of surgical drapes. Ellison and Greg Adams went to the Los Angeles garment district and found a sportswear maker to turn them into masks.
stories.quote: Greg came to Southern Cal and he and I went down to the garment district in Los Angeles, and we found a sportswear manufacturer who was going to retool their equipment
stories.why: A vivid example of improvised, real-time crisis leadership.

stories.title: Asked for advice, she hired herself
stories.summary: A CPMG pediatric leader called her for advice on setting up a hospitalist program. A day later she called back asking to apply for the job herself, and CPMG made a spot for her.
stories.quote: So I gave her advice. And, you know, I got to thinking about it, and it took me one day and I called her back and said, please let me apply for the job that you're talking about.
stories.why: Shows initiative and how a career turn can start with one call.

stories.title: Thirty-one buildings at once
stories.summary: During the financial turnaround, leadership rolled a change out to all 31 buildings instead of piloting it at three. It took about six months to undo, and she counts it among her top lessons.
stories.quote: instead of piloting it at 3 buildings, which we could have some control over, we decided to put it into 31 buildings at the same time, and that was really a mistake.
stories.why: A candid leadership lesson on piloting change before scaling it.

stories.title: Wilma, the unit secretary mentor
stories.summary: Her first real mentor was not a physician but Wilma, the unit secretary in the pediatric ICU. Wilma taught her how to deal with people and stay calm in chaos.
stories.quote: she taught me about how to deal with people and interact and calm down when things were crazy. And she was affirming and, a really, really important part of my development.
stories.why: Mentorship can come from anyone on the team, not just bosses.

stories.title: Rounding fixed the printers
stories.summary: Leadership rounding surfaced how much broken printers frustrated clinicians. CPMG launched an initiative to replace printers everywhere.
stories.quote: frankly, we've all had printer rounding, but it's sometimes your printer can ruin your whole life. And so we actually started a whole initiative to replace printers everywhere, and then that got fixed.
stories.why: Small frontline fixes build trust; listening surfaces them.

stories.title: The pre-op potassium audit
stories.summary: As quality committee chair, he wrote an audit the anesthesiology chief said was unnecessary, checking potassium before every surgery. It found unnoticed low potassium causing arrhythmias, and pre-op potassium checks became routine.
stories.quote: Let's do a pre-op potassium on every patient going to surgery. And lo and behold, we found that there were complications, arrhythmias in patients who had low K's and it wasn't being found.
stories.why: Simple quality audit that changed surgical practice and saved money

stories.title: Owning a public mistake
stories.summary: He publicly endorsed moving the cardiac surgery program from Kaiser Sunset, and the plan failed immediately. He told the medical group it was his mistake and was re-elected two years later.
stories.quote: Success has many parents okay; this one was failure. Oliver's the parent. Well, another characteristic of leadership is candor. I made the mistake. Stop there. I, Oliver, your leader, made this mistake.
stories.why: A leader's candid account of admitting error and keeping trust

stories.title: Who designed this thing? It was me
stories.summary: He championed patient assessments of physicians (MAPS) against a board member who argued for paying doctors more. Back in practice later, he found himself rated by the system he had designed.
stories.quote: it was humorous for me when I went back into practice, I began to get these assessments, and I made a lighthearted comment, who designed this thing? My patients are are evaluating me. It was me.
stories.why: Humorous origin story for patient-measured physician quality

stories.title: Edgar Kaiser and the bauxite
stories.summary: Called to treat Edgar Kaiser, he hospitalized him at Kaiser Sunset and waited while Kaiser finished a call to Jamaica. Not knowing what bauxite was, he offered to order it.
stories.quote: I'm on the phone to Jamaica. I said, Jamaica. He said, you know, bauxite and I, I didn't know and I said, bauxite. I got mixed up. I said, well, I think I can order that if you need it.
stories.why: Warm, funny first-hand encounter with Edgar Kaiser as a patient

stories.title: The NICU nurse at two a.m.
stories.summary: Less than a year into his job, after working until 2 a.m. on the EMR business case, Grant stopped at the Geary Street NICU and found a nurse rocking, feeding and singing to his premature son. He told his wife that night he had found his calling.
stories.quote: as I leaned closer, I could see that she had our son in her arms, and, um, she was feeding him, and she was rocking him, and she was actually singing to him.
stories.why: A personal origin story of KP's culture of compassion.

stories.title: Hiring the medical groups' right hands
stories.summary: Asked to strengthen the Federation, Grant asked to hire the medical groups' best people, and the medical directors agreed until they heard the names. The tension led to a design where leaders kept regional roles while serving nationally.
stories.quote: when I started to name the individuals that I thought would be great in these roles, all of a sudden, I think one by one they realized that these are our right hands.
stories.why: Shows how the Federation's distributed leadership model was born.

stories.title: No day off from March to July
stories.summary: During the pandemic Grant worked every day, including weekends, from early March through July 4th as KP planned to triple hospital capacity. He calls it exhausting but the most purposeful time, with turf wars set aside.
stories.quote: it was also the most purposeful time because, um, nobody second guessed each other. There was, um, unbelievable alignment.
stories.why: Captures how crisis aligned KP's parts around one goal.

stories.title: Three Swedish medical students
stories.summary: Planning a career in law or journalism, he spent a year in Sweden living with three medical students. Going on rounds and home visits with them convinced him medicine could best serve social justice.
stories.quote: I started going on rounds with them and especially making home visits. And, uh, I came to believe that, uh, my interest in social justice and in making the world a better place, could better be served by medicine
stories.why: Shows a chance encounter shaping a mission-driven physician career.

stories.title: "Do something about it": the white paper
stories.summary: Overworked family doctors were covering clinic, hospital rounds and urgent care. When his wife told him to stop complaining and act, he wrote a white paper proposing an urgent care department.
stories.quote: my wife said to me, well, do something about it if you feel so strongly. So I wrote a white paper, I called it a white paper, about changing and changes in medicine,
stories.why: A plain lesson in turning frustration into leadership.

stories.title: Worth half the deal: the "naked doctors"
stories.summary: During the Group Health sale, the medical group had its own investment banker ask United what its offer would be worth without the physicians. The answer was half, proving the group's value.
stories.quote: Our instructor asked our investment banker to explore with United what would the deal be worth without us? And it was literally 50% less.
stories.why: Demonstrates the power of an independent medical group in negotiations.

stories.title: The barbecue that wasn't barbecue
stories.summary: New to Georgia, she invited the chiefs to a rooftop 'barbecue' meaning only outdoor cooking. They expected Southern barbecue, and the mix-up became a shared laugh that helped build relationships.
stories.quote: In California, you call anytime you cook outside a barbecue, in Georgia, barbecue means the food barbecue. Um, and so it was hilarious. They were very disappointed.
stories.why: A warm, funny picture of a new leader building trust across cultures.

stories.title: Allergy receptionist books a life-saving mammogram
stories.summary: At Panorama City an allergy receptionist booked a reluctant patient's overdue mammogram during her allergy visit. The mammogram found breast cancer the patient says she would otherwise have missed.
stories.quote: she got her mammogram booked at her allergy appointment and it was within a couple of weeks she got it. She went to her mammogram appointment and she had breast cancer.
stories.why: Shows integrated care and proactive outreach saving a life.

stories.title: Interrupting as the only woman
stories.summary: A senior leader kindly told the young Wilson she interrupted too much in meetings. She answered that as the only woman there, she feared no one would listen otherwise.
stories.quote: I noticed you interrupt all the time in the meetings and I'm like, well, did you also notice that I'm the only woman in there? And I'm afraid nobody's going to listen to me if I don't interrupt.
stories.why: A candid, human view of gender dynamics in early physician leadership.

stories.title: Leading from where you stand
stories.summary: Frustrated by wasted time getting patients roomed, the young pediatrician walked the clinic with her nurse to find delays. A senior colleague told her to stop complaining and find a solution, and she did.
stories.quote: So we just went through and did a little efficiencies and things like that. And, um, so it's what they would later call leading from where you stand.
stories.why: Concrete model for new physicians on turning frustration into improvement.

stories.title: Secret dinners that built a dyad
stories.summary: To keep smaller Fremont from losing out on funding, Wheeler secretly met Hayward PIC Annabel Anderson-Imbert in a faraway restaurant to plan merging the two into one service area. After months with a consultant they announced the dyad, merged chief roles, and opened the long-idle Fremont hospital.
stories.quote: So I approached her confidentially to present the idea, and we met in the evening restaurant far away so that we wouldn't be discovered, etc. etc.
stories.why: Shows how a major structural change was quietly planned before going public.

stories.title: Eight former patients became physicians
stories.summary: As the only African American pediatrician in the Hayward-Oakland area, Wheeler's general pediatrics practice filled quickly. Eight of the children he cared for in those three years became physicians, including three brothers.
stories.quote: I have eight patients from my three years of doing general peds that are now physicians, three from one family, three brothers. So it was quite, quite a time to be a role model
stories.why: A concrete picture of representation and role modeling in care.

stories.title: Too nice to lead?
stories.summary: During his PIC selection, Dr. Caulfield relayed that physicians feared Wheeler was too nice to do the hard parts of leadership. Wheeler answered that leaders need not be mean-spirited and kept that question in mind when choosing other leaders.
stories.quote: physicians, they said you were such a nice guy that they didn't know that you would be able to do the hard part or the hard stuff, uh, to provide leadership.
stories.why: A memorable leadership lesson on kindness and accountability.

stories.title: Learning not to shake hands
stories.summary: At Fremont, community representatives were invited to teach staff how their communities preferred to receive care. Wheeler learned that as a male physician he should not touch Muslim mothers, changing his usual exam-room greeting.
stories.quote: my normal thing was to walk into an exam room and shake hands with the parents, say hello and then, you know, touch or interact with the child. But for Muslim women, I couldn't touch her
stories.why: A simple, teachable example of culturally responsive care.

stories.title: The $100 million back-of-envelope PACS decision
stories.summary: In 2005, when Southern California radiology said it could not afford digital imaging, Chu asked what a system-wide rollout would cost and approved $100 million on the spot. The fast rollout helped win over Permanente physicians.
stories.quote: So I said, could we do it for $100 million? So he said, um, yeah, I guess we could do it for $100 million. I said, okay, do it.
stories.why: Shows decisive health plan leadership earning physician trust.

stories.title: "Ben's kids": the case for Medicaid
stories.summary: Chu showed Jeff Weisz that falling family size meant fewer child members, so KP would either cut pediatricians or take more Medicaid children. Colleagues came to call the new members 'Ben's kids'.
stories.quote: So I said, Jeff, are you going to fire 15%, 20% of your pediatricians? I said, you know, if you if you're not going to do that, we're going to have to increase the numbers
stories.why: Mission argued through hard numbers; a memorable label for equity work.

stories.title: How POINT became CarePoint
stories.summary: After Epic went in, George Halvorson complained KP lacked real-time quality data, and for over a year Chu kept pointing to Southern California's POINT tool. Once SoCal's scores led the program, IT adopted it nationally as CarePoint.
stories.quote: every time he said that, I raised my hand and said, we do in Southern California, we have the point system.
stories.why: Shows results, not argument, spreading a regional innovation program-wide.

stories.title: A pediatrician's old stethoscope
stories.summary: Hospitalized for months at age three with rheumatic fever, Chu was given an old stethoscope by his pediatrician. His mother declared he would be a doctor.
stories.quote: one of the things she did was she gave me an old stethoscope of hers. Right. So my mother saw it and she said, oh, he's going to be a doctor. He's going to be a doctor.
stories.why: A vivid origin story about how one clinician's kindness shapes a career.

stories.title: The man behind the mask
stories.summary: On a trip to Mexico with Stanford's plastic surgery chairman, Pearl operated on an adult who had hidden his cleft lip behind a mask all his life. The 90-minute operation changed the man's life and turned Pearl toward plastic surgery.
stories.quote: I can still remember the first patient, an individual, an adult, actually, who had spent his whole life with a mask over his face. He didn't want anyone to see the cleft lip
stories.why: Shows how one patient encounter set a career's direction.

stories.title: Facing down the health plan in 1998
stories.summary: On taking the CEO role, Pearl met a health plan head who threatened to break the medical group's contracts. Pearl warned that every emergency room would close and the plan would go bankrupt, and the plan backed down.
stories.quote: And I said, I don't think you're going to do that, because as soon as you do that, every emergency room is going to close and the costs are going to be so great that you're going to go bankrupt.
stories.why: A vivid moment in the medical group-health plan partnership's history.

stories.title: From Motel6 to Johns Hopkins recruits
stories.summary: Mid-Atlantic physician recruitment had been held on Sunday afternoons at a Motel6 with chips and salsa. Pearl's team moved it to a fine Baltimore restaurant, drawing 80 Johns Hopkins attendees and 20 new physicians.
stories.quote: the way they did physician recruitment was on a Sunday afternoon at a Motel6 where they'd have some chips and salsa, and the first thing we did is we went to Baltimore
stories.why: Concrete, memorable illustration of brand-building in a struggling region.

stories.title: The paper that predicted failure
stories.summary: A friend at Berkeley's business school wrote an A-graded strategy paper concluding KP's shift to quality and service differentiation would fail. Pearl says the outcome not only matched but greatly exceeded the community.
stories.quote: And the paper was an analysis of our decision to shift the strategy. And this paper she got an A on, concluded that we would not be successful.
stories.why: Captures the risk and doubt behind the 1998 strategy shift.

stories.title: The misdirected envelope that launched EPRP
stories.summary: As emergency chief he received a stack of outside emergency claims by mistake and wrote a critique of them. That led, over years, to the Emergency Prospective Review Program and the Case Coordination Center.
stories.quote: I got the wrong envelope. Um, it somehow it got delivered to the chief of emergency medicine and what it was, was a stack of claims
stories.why: A major regional program born from an accident and persistence.

stories.title: Sidney Garfield's 2 a.m. emergency room visit
stories.summary: As a young associate on an overnight shift in San Diego, he was told a Dr. Garfield wanted to see the hospital. He showed the quiet visitor around and only later realized the significance.
stories.quote: there's a Dr. Garfield here and he'd like to see the hospital in the emergency room.
stories.why: A rare first-hand encounter with KP's founder.

stories.title: A $1,000 pension that closed a deal
stories.summary: Negotiations to bring Buena Ventura Medical Group into SCPMG were stalled until he asked in passing about their retirement plan. Learning it was $1,000, he and Greg Adams created a partnership category instead of paying cash.
stories.quote: so I asked what the retirement plan was for the shareholders, and Jim said, it's $1,000 dollars.
stories.why: Shows how partnership benefits, not cash, won an acquisition.

stories.title: Approving an unbudgeted $55 million vaccine
stories.summary: When the HPV vaccine was approved mid-year, physicians asked to start giving it at an unbudgeted cost of $55 million. He approved it on the spot because the risk sharing arrangement would return most of any shortfall.
stories.quote: it was going to be a $55 million hit. And I think it was April, early in the year it was going to be, and we didn't think about it more than, I said, go ahead, do it.
stories.why: Concrete example of aligned incentives enabling quality decisions.

stories.title: A doctor, not a dentist
stories.summary: At about 12 or 13, walking to the mailbox, his father steered him from dentistry to medicine. He says he would choose the career again.
stories.quote: I remember walking out to the mailbox with my dad when I was about 12 or 13 years old. He said, so what do you want to do with yourself? I said, I think I'll become a dentist.
stories.why: A vivid, human origin story for a physician career.

stories.title: Why are you at Kaiser?
stories.summary: Early in his career, patients asked why such a caring doctor wasn't in private practice. He describes how SCPMG's reputation later changed, until UCLA residents wanted to join.
stories.quote: patients would walk in and say to me, why are you at Kaiser Permanente? You seem so personable. You seem so caring. How come you're not out in private practice?
stories.why: Shows how KP's public image shifted over decades.

stories.title: Told to get lost over EMR
stories.summary: When he announced the electronic medical record, physicians and the board nearly threw him out of the room. He phased it in one medical center at a time and credits it with transforming care.
stories.quote: I told our physicians and the board that we're bringing electronic medical record, they almost, you know, took me out of the room and told me to get lost. Okay. You're out of here.
stories.why: Captures resistance to a now-essential change.

stories.title: Someone from the major leagues
stories.summary: Past SCPMG's retirement age, he was recruited to Northwest Permanente, which had no age limit. He cut its outside medical expense from $55 million to $25 million in four years.
stories.quote: I remember they said, hey, do you want someone from the minor leagues or do you want someone from the major leagues, who played major league ball? That was me.
stories.why: A memorable second act after mandatory retirement.

stories.title: Delivered through the nursery drawer
stories.summary: Minardi was born in 1955 at KP's Los Angeles Medical Center, where newborns were passed to mothers through a wall drawer. His mother retold the story every birthday, including sending him back through the drawer so she could rest.
stories.quote: she would recollect the story of being delivered to her through the drawer by the nurses.
stories.why: A narrator's own birth illustrates a famous KP care-design innovation.

stories.title: Delivering babies in Mexican hamlets
stories.summary: As a medical student in Guadalajara he helped deliver care in small villages with no health care, including home births. The families' gratitude, with no money exchanged, shaped his choice of a prepaid, mission-driven practice.
stories.quote: we delivered babies in patients homes, um, use whatever utility there was, uh, at the time, in addition to what we brought with us
stories.why: Shows how early service far from money shaped his values.

stories.title: The dinner that dissolved the MSAs
stories.summary: At a dinner with Mr. Cordova and Greg Adams, Jeff Weisz had Minardi explain why Southern California's Medical Service Areas were dysfunctional. Shortly afterward the MSAs were dissolved.
stories.quote: I remember their faces that night because I couldn't believe what we were suggesting, but shortly thereafter we did that. We dissolved the MSAs.
stories.why: A vivid moment when one argument changed regional structure.

stories.title: Don't go on your own, Greg
stories.summary: In a weekly call after the pandemic, KP CEO Greg Adams said the health plan might pursue national growth without Permanente. Minardi proposed doing it together, which led to the KP Medical Foundation.
stories.quote: So Greg said, I'm going to go on my own. And I offered to him an opportunity that said, Greg, don't go on your own, but let's think about how we do this together
stories.why: Origin story of the KP Medical Foundation, told by its co-creator.
